locations.name: Toowoomba
locations.depot: Loaded at our Lockyer Valley yard, at the bottom of the range
locations.leadTime: Commonly next business day, and rarely more than three
locations.truck: Tilt-tray handles 10ft and 20ft; a 40ft goes on a side loader, or a crane truck where the block is tight
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Toowoomba. Hauled up the range from our Lockyer Valley yard, with real advice on black soil, streets and frost.
locations.line: Toowoomba sits about 700 metres above the coastal plain, so every container that lands here has been hauled up a range to get there. That part is routine for us, because we load at the bottom of it. The harder half is the ground: black soil that greases up in the wet and opens into cracks in the dry, and old streets with big trees leaning over them.
locations.uses: trade storage for builders working across the Garden City suburbs, secure lock-ups on renovation sites where the old shed came down before the new one went up, machinery and chemical storage on the acreage out through Highfields, Meringandan and Westbrook, feed and fencing gear on the smaller grazing blocks south toward Cambooya, and overflow storage for the freight and logistics yards that have grown up around Charlton and Wellcamp
access:
There are two ways up and the truck takes whichever suits the load. The old range road out of Withcott is short, steep and tight, with a grade that has been punishing brakes since long before any of us were driving. Most heavy vehicles now run the Toowoomba Bypass instead, which swings north around the city and comes in near Charlton. Either way the container arrives having climbed the better part of 700 metres, and that is the easy part.

The real problem in Toowoomba is under your feet. The Downs black soil is a reactive clay. Wet, it turns to grease and a loaded truck will cut ruts a foot deep and then sit in them while you go and find a tractor. Dry, it shrinks and splits, and cracks wide enough to swallow a boot will open right where you wanted the container to sit. Neither state is a reason to cancel, but both are a reason to talk about timing and about exactly where the unit goes. On black soil we want the container on the highest, firmest line available, with a few sleepers or a run of road base under the corner castings so the load has something to spread into.

The established suburbs bring their own trouble. East Toowoomba, Rangeville and the streets running down toward the escarpment are steep, kerbed and heavily treed, and the canopy this city is known for sits lower over the bitumen than people think. A tilt-tray needs a clear vertical envelope a long way above the container while the tray is up. Add parked cars on a narrow street and the practical answer is often an early start before the school run. Out at Highfields, Westbrook and Gowrie Junction the blocks are bigger and the driveways longer, which helps, until a wet week makes a gravel entry soft. Winter is quietly the best season to deliver here, because a hard frost sets the ground up beautifully.

sections.h: What 700 metres of altitude does inside the box
p: Winter up here does something to a steel box that people on the coast never have to think about. A clear night on the Downs drops hard, frost on the grass by five in the morning, and then the afternoon comes back mild. The steel follows the air temperature almost instantly. The contents do not. Whatever moisture is in the air inside condenses on the underside of the roof and runs down the walls, and if the box is packed tight it can drip onto the top of the stack for weeks before anyone notices. It is not a leak, and no amount of sealing fixes it. People call it container rain, and it is the single most common thing we hear back about from the Downs, far more than anything to do with weather getting in from outside.

The cure is airflow and dry loading. Every unit comes with vents in the top rails, and on a container that is going to sit closed for months on a Toowoomba block we would rather see more of them, plus a whirlybird if the contents are worth protecting. Set the unit on hardwood sleepers or concrete pads under the corner castings so air moves underneath and the floor is not sitting in a puddle. Get it level, or as near as the ground allows, so the doors line up and the seals do their job. Do not load hay, green timber, damp carpet or anything else with water still in it and then shut the doors, because the moisture has to go somewhere. If you are storing something that really hates damp, a bucket of desiccant costs almost nothing and works. None of this is exotic. It is just the difference between a dry box and a wet one.

sections.h: Two Toowoombas: kerbside in town, paddock gate out west
p: In town the constraint is almost never the container, it is the run-up. A tilt-tray puts a 20ft on the ground by raising the tray and letting the unit slide off the back, and it needs roughly twice the length of the box in clear straight ground to do it. So a 20ft wants somewhere around twelve metres, and it wants that in a line, not around a corner. On the older streets between the CBD and the escarpment that line is often the road rather than the block, which means a few minutes of traffic management and a neighbour or two moving a car. Check the driveway crossover as well, because a lot of the older kerbing in this city was poured for a family sedan rather than for a rigid truck carrying a container, and a cracked crossover is an argument nobody wants to have.

Out through Highfields, Meringandan, Gowrie Junction, Hodgson Vale and Westbrook the space stops being the issue and the surface starts. Long gravel drives soften fast after a wet week, entry culverts are often a couple of pipes and some fill that nobody has ever load-rated, and farm gates get built to the width of the ute that goes through them daily rather than the width of a truck. Overhanging limbs are the other one. The five minutes worth having is a walk from the road to the spot with a tape and a phone, looking up as much as down, and a photo or two sent through before the truck is loaded. We would far rather redesign the approach in the office than turn a semi around in somebody's house paddock.

sections.h: Which grade earns its keep on the Downs
p: Grade matters more here than in a mild coastal climate, because the swings are bigger and the box has nothing over it. A cargo-worthy unit is one assessed as fit to carry freight at sea, and every cargo-worthy container we send out is checked wind and watertight before it leaves the yard. That is the grade to buy if the contents matter and the unit is living outside on a Toowoomba block. One-trip units are a step up again in cosmetic condition and door seal, and they are what most people choose when the container is going somewhere visible, or is going to be cut into later. As-is units are the cheaper end of the market and they are exactly what the name says: sold in the condition they stand in, not sold as watertight, and perfectly good for a hay store, a fence-line lock-up or a job where a bit of daylight through a roof seam does not matter. We will tell you plainly which grade a unit is, and you are welcome to drive down the range and look at it on the hardstand before it goes on a truck.

faqs.q: Do you come up the old range road or use the Toowoomba Bypass?
faqs.a: Whichever suits the load and the traffic on the day. The bypass takes heavy vehicles around the north of the city and joins the highway out near Charlton, and it is the steadier climb, so most of our Toowoomba loads go that way. The old range road out of Withcott is shorter, but it is steep and tight and it is no place for a truck carrying a 40ft when there is an alternative. Either way the container has climbed close to 700 metres by the time it reaches you, and that part is our problem rather than yours.

faqs.q: Can a container be delivered onto black soil after rain?
faqs.a: Sometimes, and sometimes it is a very bad idea. Downs black soil is a reactive clay that drains slowly, so a day or two after decent rain the surface turns greasy and a loaded truck will cut ruts you will be looking at all summer. If the spot is off hardstand and it has been wet, we will usually suggest moving the delivery a few days, or placing the unit on the firmest ground we can reach and repositioning it later with a machine. Nobody wins from a bogged truck in your paddock.

faqs.q: How long does it take to get a container to Toowoomba?
faqs.a: Usually the next business day, and rarely more than three. Our yard is at Forest Hill in the Lockyer Valley, roughly forty-five minutes down the range from the Toowoomba CBD, so this is a short run for us rather than a country freight job. The timing that matters more is at your end: confirming where the unit is going, what the approach looks like and whether the ground is dry. Ring in the morning with that sorted and there is a fair chance it is on the ground the following day.

faqs.q: Can I inspect a container before it is trucked up to Toowoomba?
faqs.a: Yes, and plenty of Toowoomba people do. The yard is at Forest Hill, straight down the range and along the highway, and the units sit on hardstand where you can walk them, open the doors, check the floor and pick the one you want. Ring first so we know you are coming and can have the right sizes accessible. If the drive is not worth it, photos of the actual unit are available on request and before delivery, but the trip takes under an hour each way and it settles the question properly.

locations.name: Gatton
locations.depot: Our own hardstand at Forest Hill, ten minutes down the road
locations.leadTime: Frequently the same day when the unit is ready and the truck is free, otherwise next morning
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft, side loader for 40ft, all of it dispatched from the yard up the road
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Gatton. Our yard is ten minutes away at Forest Hill, so you can come and walk the rows before your unit is loaded.
locations.line: Gatton is about as close as this job gets. Our yard sits at Forest Hill, ten minutes east on the Forest Hill Fernvale Road, which means the haul is short, the freight component is small, and you can drive out, walk the rows and put your hand on the actual container before anyone loads it. The complication here is not distance. It is irrigated ground.
locations.uses: packing shed overflow through the vegetable season, secure storage for irrigation fittings, poly and drip tape that tends to walk if it is left in the open, chemical and fertiliser lock-ups a sensible distance from the main shed, dry storage for bins, crates and pallets between plantings, machinery and header parts on the grain country south of town, and tool storage for the trades working around the university campus and the newer estates
access:
The Lockyer floor is deep alluvial soil that has been worked, watered and cultivated for a century, and it behaves nothing like the hard country either side of it. Dry, a cultivated headland will carry a truck happily. Two days after an irrigation run or a decent storm, the same headland turns into a paste that a loaded rigid will sink through in one wheel rotation. This is the single thing we ask about before a Gatton delivery: has that paddock had water on it this week. It is not a hard question to answer and it saves everybody a bad afternoon.

Farm access here also tends to run through infrastructure rather than around it. Irrigation channels, buried mainline, lay-flat across a track, a pump shed at the pinch point, a lateral move parked where the truck needs to swing. Steel does not care, but a mainline under 200mm of soil does, and a set of dual wheels with a container on the tray will find it. We would rather come in the long way through a gate that looks inconvenient than take the short way over a pipe.

In town the picture flips. The older blocks around the main street are compact, with a single driveway, a fence line and a clothesline exactly where the container wants to go, and the practical answer is often to place it in the front yard and move it later with a smaller machine.

Then there is water. Lockyer Creek has been through this town more than once and everyone here knows their own contour better than any map. We will not pretend a container solves that. What it does is hold your gear at whatever height you put it, so if there is a rise on the block, that is where the unit goes, and it is worth spending an extra half hour getting the pad right rather than putting it on the low corner because the truck can reach it easily.

sections.h: Ten minutes away, and what that actually buys you
p: The distance between the yard at Forest Hill and most of Gatton is about ten minutes, and that changes the shape of the whole transaction. You are not buying a container off a photo and a description and hoping for the best. Ring, tell us what you are after, and drive out. The units sit on hardstand in rows and you can walk them, open the doors, look along the floor, put a torch on the roof seams and decide which particular box you want. People do it on a lunch break. The unit you looked at is the unit that gets loaded, which sounds like it should be normal and is not always.

A short haul also means the delivery is a small part of the number rather than the thing that decides it, and it means we can be flexible in ways a long-distance carrier cannot. If the first position does not work once the truck is on site, and sometimes it does not, because a spot that looked fine from the kitchen window turns out to have a septic trench under it, we are ten minutes from home rather than four hours. Photos of the unit are available on request and before delivery if you would rather not come out at all. But for a Gatton job, coming out is better, and most people do.

sections.h: Containers in a working vegetable operation
p: Vegetable growing in this valley runs hard for months and then stops, and the storage problem follows exactly the same shape. Through the season the packing shed is full and there is nowhere to put the things that are not needed this week. Out of season there is a mountain of gear, including bins, crates, pallets, shade cloth, drip tape, fittings and spare pump ends, that has to live somewhere dry and out of the sun, because ultraviolet destroys poly faster than use does. A container parked at the end of the shed solves both, and unlike a farm shed it locks properly and it can be shifted to the next block if the operation moves.

The second job it does out here is keeping things away from the main shed. Chemical, fertiliser, fuel gear and spray equipment are all better off in their own lockable steel box a sensible distance from where people work and where machinery is parked, and a container gives you that without adding another permanent building to the yard. If it is going to hold anything that gasses off, vent it properly and vent it high. That is a cheap addition while the unit is in front of us at the yard and an awkward one afterwards. Vermin are the other reality. A container sitting level with intact door seals and a solid floor is genuinely hard for rats and mice to get into, which is more than most sheds around here can claim.

sections.h: Why level matters more on cultivated ground
p: A shipping container gets its strength from its corners, and it wants those four corners supported and roughly in the same plane. On the cultivated flats around Gatton the soil is soft, deep and worked, and a container sitting straight on it will settle unevenly over a season, usually one corner more than the rest. When it does, the frame racks a fraction and the doors stop meeting. Anyone who has fought a container door that will not close on a hot afternoon has met this problem. The fix costs almost nothing at delivery and is a genuine pain later: put something under the corners. Hardwood sleepers, concrete pads, even a couple of well-bedded blocks per corner will do it, set on ground scraped back to something firm rather than on loose topsoil. Get that right on day one and the doors will still line up in five years.

faqs.q: Can I come and look at containers near Gatton before I buy one?
faqs.a: Yes. The yard is at Forest Hill, about ten minutes from the centre of Gatton on the Forest Hill Fernvale Road, and the stock sits on hardstand in rows. Ring before you come so someone is there and so we can have the sizes you are interested in where you can get to them. You can open doors, look along the roof seams, check the floor and settle on a specific unit. The one you pick is the one that gets loaded. Weekday mornings are the quietest time to come out.

faqs.q: How fast can you get a container onto a farm near Gatton?
faqs.a: Often the same day if the unit is on the ground, the truck is free and the access is sorted, and the next morning if it is not. Ten minutes of driving does not take much organising. What slows a Gatton delivery down is almost never the distance. It is finding out on arrival that the paddock had water on it this week, or that the gate is narrower than the truck. Answer those two on the phone and this is about as quick as container delivery gets anywhere.

faqs.q: Will a container sit safely on cultivated ground?
faqs.a: It will, provided you put something under the corners. A container carries its weight through the four corner castings, and on deep worked Lockyer soil those corners will press in unevenly over a season if they are sitting straight on dirt. When one corner drops, the frame twists slightly and the doors stop meeting. Scrape back to firm ground and set hardwood sleepers, concrete pads or well-bedded blocks under each corner. It takes twenty minutes at delivery and it is the difference between doors that still line up in five years and doors you have to lift.

faqs.q: Is the yard open on Saturday?
faqs.a: Saturday mornings, 8am to 12pm, and Monday to Friday 7:30am to 5pm. Saturday suits people who cannot get away during the week and it is a reasonable time to come and look at stock, though it is worth ringing ahead either way so we know to expect you and can have units accessible. Deliveries are generally weekday work. If you want to look on a Saturday and have it delivered early the following week, that sequence works well and it is what a lot of local buyers do.

locations.name: Laidley
locations.depot: Loaded at our Forest Hill yard, a few minutes up the road
locations.leadTime: Usually next business day, and often the same day when the yard has the unit ready
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; a 40ft goes out on a side loader, because a lot of entries here will not take a semi turning
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Laidley. Short haul from our Forest Hill yard, with honest advice on narrow blocks, creek crossings and wet ground.
locations.line: Laidley is close enough to the yard that our trucks pass through it on the way to somewhere else. That helps. What does not help is the town itself, which was laid out long before anybody was reversing a twelve-metre tray down a driveway, and the creek, which has been through the middle of it more than once.
locations.uses: storage on the smaller mixed farms out toward Mulgowie, Thornton and Blenheim, turf and machinery gear, hay and feed under lock, workshop and tool storage for tradesmen working out of home blocks in town, clean dry space through a rebuild or a renovation, and secure storage on the rural-residential blocks up around Laidley Heights where the shed has not been built yet
access:
Two different delivery problems share one postcode here. In town the blocks are old, deep and narrow, with a single driveway down one side and often a carport, a tank or a side gate halfway along it that stops a truck dead. Where there is rear lane access it is usually the answer, but the lanes are narrow and the fences are close, and it is worth a look at the aerial before we commit a tilt-tray to going down one. Where there is not, the container frequently goes in the front yard on the day and gets walked around later with a machine. That is a normal outcome in Laidley, not a failure.

Out in the valley the constraints are the roads. Mulgowie, Thornton, Townson and the country up the creek are served by narrow sealed roads that go to gravel, with floodways and low causeways at the crossings and not much shoulder to pull onto. A loaded truck cannot simply stop and turn around out there, so we plan the run knowing where it can turn before it commits. After rain the causeways decide the day rather than the paddock. If water is over a crossing the delivery moves, and that is not a negotiation.

The ground on the valley floor is good alluvial soil that grows things well and holds water for exactly the same reason. Dry, it is firm and a truck will drive on it happily. Wet, it goes greasy on top while staying solid underneath, which is the worst combination of the two, because it looks fine right up until the wheels break traction on a slope.

Laidley Creek has been through the town more than once and the people here know their contours better than we do. Where a block has any rise on it, that is where the container goes, and we would rather spend the extra ten minutes getting to the high corner than the easy one.

sections.h: Hiring versus buying on a short job
p: The question comes up on almost every renovation and rebuild in this district, and the answer is usually about time rather than money. If the storage need has an end date, a kitchen out for six weeks, a roof off, a shed being replaced, a house being lifted, then hire is the cleaner arrangement. The unit arrives, does the job, and goes away again, and nobody is left owning a steel box they now have to sell or find a use for.

If the need does not have an end date, buying wins fairly quickly. Storage on a rural block is rarely temporary. The gear that has to go somewhere this year still has to go somewhere in five years. A purchased unit also stays on the block and keeps working, becoming the fencing store, the feed shed or the workshop annexe, and it holds a resale value that a shed does not. The honest test is whether you can name the date you will not need it any more. If you can, hire it. If you cannot, buy it, and put it somewhere you will still be happy with it permanently.

sections.h: Security on a block nobody watches at night
p: Theft around the valley is opportunistic and it goes for the things that are easy to lift and easy to sell: power tools, generators, welders, fuel, chainsaws, quad bikes, copper. A container beats every alternative here for one plain reason. There is nothing to lever. A shed has sheeting, a roller door and a personal access door, all of which give somebody something to work with. A container is a welded steel box with two doors on solid locking bars, and getting into one without keys and a plan is genuinely hard work.

The weak point is the padlock, so protect it. A lockbox welded over the lock area shrouds the shackle so bolt cutters cannot reach it, and it is worth the small cost on any unit holding tools. Beyond that, orientation does a lot of free work. Put the doors facing the house, or facing a fence line, or into a corner where a vehicle cannot back up to them. Somebody who cannot get a ute to the doors is not carrying a welder across a paddock in the dark. Light the approach if there is power nearby. None of it is high technology. It just makes your place the harder option.

sections.h: Ten foot or twenty on a town block
p: Most Laidley town blocks will take a 20ft comfortably once it is in position. Getting it into position is what decides things. A 20ft is about six metres long and two and a half wide, and it wants roughly twelve metres of straight clear ground to be tilted off, which on a deep narrow block usually means the front yard or the road. A 10ft is a little over three metres long, takes far less room to place, fits down the side of most houses, and is enough for a mower, tools, garden gear and a stack of boxes. It is also much easier to move later. Where the block is tight and the need is domestic, the 10ft is very often the right answer even though the 20ft looks like better value per square metre. Where a trailer, a bike or building materials are involved, the 20ft earns its space. Either way, measure the approach before you decide on the size rather than after.

faqs.q: Will a truck get a container down a Laidley driveway?
faqs.a: Often, but the older town blocks make it a real question rather than a formality. The typical Laidley house block is deep and narrow with a single drive down one side, and a carport, a tank or a side gate halfway along stops a tilt-tray well before the back yard. Where there is rear lane access, that is usually the answer. Where there is not, we place the unit at the front and it gets walked around later with a machine. Send through a couple of photos and we will tell you which one it will be.

faqs.q: Do you deliver out to Mulgowie, Thornton and Blenheim?
faqs.a: Yes. That country is close to the yard and we are on those roads regularly. The planning is about the roads rather than the distance. The valley roads narrow and go to gravel, there are floodways and causeways at the creek crossings, and there is nowhere for a loaded truck to turn around between certain points, so the run gets worked out before it leaves rather than on the fly. If the crossings are up, the delivery moves to the next dry day. That is not caution, it is the only sensible way to do it.

faqs.q: What happens if the creek crossings are up on my delivery day?
faqs.a: We move it, and we will ring you rather than wait for you to ring us. A loaded truck on a flooded causeway is not a risk anybody in this business takes. Water through the Laidley and Lockyer crossings usually drops away fast once the rain stops, so it tends to be a matter of days rather than weeks. If the delivery is time-critical, tell us at the point of order and we will build a bit of room into the date rather than promising something the weather can take away from both of us.

faqs.q: Where should a container go on a block that has had water through it?
faqs.a: On the highest firm ground you have, with the doors reachable from that same high side. A container will not keep floodwater out. Water reaches the door seals and comes in, and an empty unit will float, so the only thing protecting what is inside is the height you put it at. People in Laidley generally know their own contour better than any map does, so back your own judgement. It is worth building the pad up and spending the extra time getting the truck to the high corner rather than the easy one.

locations.name: Esk
locations.depot: Out of the Lockyer yard and up the Brisbane Valley Highway
locations.leadTime: Usually two to three business days
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; a 40ft on a side loader where the entry allows it, which on ridge blocks it often does not
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Esk and the Brisbane Valley. Delivered from our Lockyer yard, with real detail on ridge driveways, grids and gravel.
locations.line: Esk is about forty-five minutes north of the yard, straight up the Brisbane Valley Highway, and it is genuinely different country to the Lockyer flats we load on. Ridges, timber, cattle and lifestyle blocks. The container is the easy part. Getting the truck to the right spot on the block is where the thinking goes.
locations.uses: hay, feed and fencing gear on the grazing country either side of the valley, saddlery and stock equipment where the tack room has run out, quad bikes, side-by-sides and pumps kept out of the weather and under a lock, building materials on rural blocks where a house or shed is going up in stages, storage for the accommodation and tourism operators along the rail trail, and general lock-up on lifestyle acreage that has not got a shed yet
access:
Almost everything difficult about an Esk delivery happens in the last four hundred metres. The highway run is easy, sealed the whole way, no range crossing, a steady climb up the valley. Then the truck turns off onto a gravel road and everything changes.

Rural driveways around Esk, Toogoolawah, Coominya and the country up toward the dam tend to come off ridge roads and drop away, sometimes sharply. A steep driveway is not automatically a problem, but a steep driveway with a tight bend in it usually is, because a tilt-tray needs to be square to the drop-off point and the tray angle has to work with the slope rather than against it. Delivering downhill onto a fall also means the container wants to keep going once it starts moving. We would rather place the unit at the top near the road, or on the first flat bench we find, than take a truck somewhere it cannot back out of.

Cattle grids are the other classic. Most of them were built decades ago for a tractor and a stock truck and nobody has ever put a rating on one. If there is a gate beside the grid, we will use the gate. If there is not, tell us before the truck is loaded rather than when it is sitting at your entrance.

Then there is timber. Ridge driveways here run through gums that have been there a lot longer than the driveway, and the branch that clears a stock crate by half a metre will not clear a raised tilt tray. Vertical clearance is the thing people forget to check, every single time. Gravel gets chewed up after rain and takes a while to come back, and the same wet spell that softens a paddock makes the drainage crossings on those roads rough enough to matter. A dry week is worth waiting for out here.

sections.h: Buying for a block with nothing on it yet
p: The pattern around Esk and up through the valley is familiar. Somebody buys forty acres, the house or the shed is a year or two away, and in the meantime there is fencing wire, a mower, a pump, tools, a chainsaw and half a demolished kitchen sitting under a tarp. A container solves that stage properly. It arrives complete, it locks, it does not need power, water, a slab or a builder, and it can be on the block before anything else is. The trick is to put it where it will still make sense in three years rather than where the truck could reach easily on the day, because moving it later means another truck.

Think about the finished layout first. Most people end up wanting the container near where the shed will eventually go, square to it, with a clear vehicle approach and the doors on the sheltered side. Keep it off any line where a driveway, a trench or a tank will eventually run, and leave enough space to walk right around it, because you will want to at some point and a container jammed against a boundary fence is impossible to maintain and a nuisance to shift. If the block has a rise on it, the top of that rise is almost always the right answer for drainage as well as for access.

sections.h: Grass fire season and clearance
p: The valley cures off through spring and grass fires are a normal part of the year here, not an exception. A container is steel, so it will not burn, but that is not the same as being safe in a fire and we would never suggest it is. A grass fire running under and around a unit will take the paint, cook the door seals and can absolutely destroy what is inside, because a closed steel box in a fire front becomes an oven long before anything catches alight. Treat it the way you would treat any structure on the block. Keep the grass down around it, keep it clear of a timber line and out of a fuel-loaded gully, and do not park it anywhere you would not put a shed. Clearance is worth more than anything you can buy with the container, and it costs an hour with a slasher.

sections.h: Hay, feed and the things that come to eat it
p: Grazing blocks up the valley use containers mostly for the same short list. Baled hay and feed, fencing gear, water fittings, drench and vet supplies, tools, and the bikes and side-by-sides that are too valuable to leave in an open bay. All of it goes in well, with one condition. It has to go in dry. Hay put away with any moisture still in it will sweat inside a closed steel box, and in a valley that fogs most winter mornings there is already plenty of moisture in the air to work with.

Rodents are the other constant. A container that is level, with door seals in one piece and no rust holes along the floor line, is a much harder proposition for mice and rats than a pole shed with a gap under every sheet. But a unit sitting crooked on soft ground opens a gap at one corner, and that is all they need. Set it on sleepers or pads at the four corners, check it once after the first wet season, and pack it so there is air around the stack rather than filling it to the roof. A pallet on the floor under anything valuable is cheap insurance in a place where the ground stays damp for months.

faqs.q: Can a container be delivered down a steep driveway near Esk?
faqs.a: Usually, with a look at it first. Slope on its own is manageable. Slope with a bend in it is the problem, because a tilt-tray has to be square to the spot and the tray angle has to work with the fall rather than against it. Delivering downhill also means the unit wants to keep moving once it starts to slide. Often the sensible answer is to place it on the first flat bench off the road rather than at the bottom. Send photos of the driveway from both ends before the truck is loaded and we will tell you honestly.

faqs.q: Can we use a container for storage while we build on a rural block?
faqs.a: It is one of the main reasons people out this way buy one. It arrives complete, it locks, and it needs no power, water or slab, so it can be on the block before anything else is. Put it where it will still make sense once the house and shed are up rather than where the truck could reach most easily on the day, because moving it later means another truck. Leave room to walk right around it, and keep it off any line where a driveway, trench or tank will eventually run.

faqs.q: Do you deliver to Toogoolawah, Coominya, Lowood and Harlin?
faqs.a: Yes, all of it, and it is the same road for most of the way. The Brisbane Valley Highway carries our trucks from the Lockyer up through Fernvale and Lowood and on to Esk and Toogoolawah, so those places sit on a straightforward route. Harlin and the country further up takes a bit longer but is no harder. As always the last few hundred metres decide the day rather than the highway, so the useful information is about your gate, your driveway and what is overhead, not about the distance.

faqs.q: Do I need a concrete pad, or will gravel do, on a sloping block?
faqs.a: Gravel is fine, and so is bare ground, as long as the four corners are supported and roughly level. A slab is not required and is rarely worth pouring just for a container. What matters is that the corner castings sit on something that will not sink: hardwood sleepers, concrete pads or well-bedded blocks, set on ground scraped back to firm material rather than on topsoil. On a slope you build the low side up rather than digging the high side out, and you check it again after the first wet season.

locations.name: Fernvale
locations.depot: Our Forest Hill yard, at the southern end of the Forest Hill Fernvale Road
locations.leadTime: Usually one to two business days; it is a half-hour run each way
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; side loader for 40ft, which suits the newer acreage estates where there is room to work
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Fernvale. Our yard sits on the Forest Hill Fernvale Road, so it is a short run to your acreage block or estate.
locations.line: There is a road called the Forest Hill Fernvale Road and our yard sits on it. That is the whole story of how close this is: about twenty-five minutes, one road, no range crossing and no city traffic. What makes Fernvale interesting is not the haul. It is that half the blocks here are five years old and the other half are a hundred.
locations.uses: storage on the new acreage estates around Vernor, Glamorgan Vale and Wivenhoe Pocket while a shed is designed and built, tool and trade storage for the many people here who work in Ipswich or Brisbane and run a business off the block, horse and stock gear, mower and machinery cover, dry space through a renovation, and secure overflow for the small businesses along the highway
access:
Fernvale has been subdividing for years and the newest estates bring a specific delivery problem: the ground is not old enough. A driveway that was poured or gravelled six months ago sits on fill that has not been through a full wet season, and the batters either side of it are still finding their angle. A truck with a container on the back is a genuine load test. Where the driveway is new we place the unit close to the hardstand at the top rather than driving the length of it, and where the crossover is fresh concrete we will ask about the pour date, because a heavy vehicle on green concrete is a repair bill with a truck parked next to it.

The blocks themselves are usually generous, which is the good news. One and two acre lots give a side loader room to work, and a side loader puts a container down neatly into a defined footprint without needing the long straight run-off a tilt-tray wants. Where landscaping is already in, it is worth thinking about the approach beforehand: new turf marks badly, irrigation on a new lawn is shallow, and silt fencing and star pickets do not survive contact with a truck.

The older country is different again. The river flats down toward Lowood and along the Brisbane River are alluvial and soft after rain, and the low ridges are reactive clay that heaves. Neither is a reason to avoid a spot, but both are a reason to put something solid under the corners rather than sitting the box on grass and hoping.

The last practical thing is the highway. The Brisbane Valley Highway through Fernvale carries a heavy commuter flow morning and evening and it gets busy through the middle of the day on weekends. An early delivery slot is easier on everyone, and it is usually easier to get.

sections.h: Storage while the shed is still a drawing
p: A lot of Fernvale blocks follow the same sequence. The land settles, the house goes up, and the shed, which is the thing everybody actually wanted, is the last item and the one that gets deferred. In between there is a garage full of things that should be in a shed, a mower under a tarp and a trailer living on the lawn. A container covers that gap and it is not a compromise. It is dry, it locks, it is on the block in a day, and it holds its value if you sell it on afterwards. Plenty of people who bought one as a stopgap end up keeping it and putting the shed somewhere else entirely.

If it is a stopgap, put it where a truck can get back to it. That sounds obvious and it is regularly ignored. A container placed behind a house, past a new retaining wall and a set of garden beds, is a genuinely difficult thing to recover. Leave a straight approach from the driveway, keep landscaping out of that path until the container is gone, and if the block is still bare, take a photo of where the services run before the turf goes down. It costs nothing now and saves an argument with an excavator later.

sections.h: Tilt-tray or side loader on an acreage block
p: These are two different machines that put a container on the ground two different ways, and which one suits depends on the block rather than the container. A tilt-tray raises its tray and slides the unit off the back. It is simple, it is quick and it is the usual choice for 10ft and 20ft units, but it needs a straight clear run roughly twice the length of the container to do it, and it needs vertical clearance well above the box while the tray is up. On a wide Fernvale acreage block that is rarely a problem. On a narrow older lot with a carport and a mature tree it can be the whole problem.

A side loader carries the container alongside the truck on two hydraulic lifting arms and sets it down beside itself. It does not need the long run-off, it can place a unit into a defined footprint with real precision, and it is generally how a 40ft gets delivered. What it does need is enough width to park square to the spot and enough firm ground under the truck to take the load while it lifts. On new estate blocks with a big cleared area it is usually the easier of the two. Tell us what the spot looks like and we will send the right truck rather than the one that happens to be free. That decision gets made in the office and it is the main thing that stops a delivery going wrong.

sections.h: Which way the doors should face
p: Orientation gets decided in about ten seconds on delivery day and then lived with for years, so it is worth thinking about beforehand. Point the doors away from the weather that actually arrives, which around here means the driving rain that comes with a southerly or a westerly change, because a container with its doors into that gets water sitting in the door sill after every storm. Afternoon sun on the door end ages the seals faster and makes the box unpleasant to open in February. Beyond weather, face the doors toward the way you will approach with a vehicle, because carrying things around the long side of a 20ft is a surprisingly tedious walk. Take five minutes with a tape before the truck arrives and mark the four corners with pegs. It is the cheapest possible way to avoid moving it again.

faqs.q: Will a delivery truck damage a new driveway on an estate block?
faqs.a: It can, and it is worth talking about before the day rather than after. New driveways sit on fill that has not been through a wet season, and fresh concrete crossovers do not like heavy vehicles at all, so if yours has been poured in the last month, tell us. Where the driveway is new we would rather place the container near the top on established hardstand than drive its full length. If the block is still bare, the whole question usually goes away and we can drive straight to the spot.

faqs.q: How quickly can you get a container to Fernvale?
faqs.a: Usually one to two business days. The yard is at Forest Hill on the Forest Hill Fernvale Road, which is named for the two ends of it, and the run is about twenty-five minutes with no range crossing and no city traffic. That short haul means we can be flexible about timing, including an early slot before the highway fills with commuter traffic, which is generally the easiest time of day to be putting a truck across a driveway on that side of town.

faqs.q: Can we get a container onto the block before the house is built?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is often the easiest kind of delivery we do, because the block is clear and the truck can drive to the spot without threading past landscaping. There is no need for power, water or an address plate. The two things to check are that the access off the road is trafficable for a heavy vehicle rather than just a ute, and that the ground where the unit will sit is firm and reasonably level. Set the corners on sleepers or pads and it will stay square right through the build.

faqs.q: How much room do the doors need to open?
faqs.a: More than most people expect. A container door swings well past ninety degrees, so you want roughly two metres of clear unobstructed ground off the door end, plus room to stand and work. If the unit is going against a fence, put the doors away from the fence. If it is going beside a shed, check that the shed roller door and the container doors are not going to fight each other. It is a ten-second decision on delivery day that you then live with for years, so make it beforehand.

locations.name: Warwick
locations.depot: Loaded in the Lockyer Valley and run south, either over the Gap or down the New England
locations.leadTime: Usually three to five business days
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; 40ft on a side loader, which the wide streets and long rural entries here suit
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Warwick and the Southern Downs. Real advice on the Gap, black soil, granite country and delivering through a frost.
locations.line: Two roads get a container to Warwick and neither of them is dull. The Cunningham Highway climbs Cunninghams Gap through the Main Range, narrow, steep and occasionally shut. The alternative is up the Toowoomba range and down the New England, longer but steadier. Once the truck is on the Downs flats around Warwick, the delivery itself is usually the easiest part of the day.
locations.uses: cattle and horse gear on the grazing country either side of the Condamine, saddlery, campdraft and rodeo equipment that has to travel and then be stored, grain, seed and fodder under lock, workshop and machinery storage on cropping blocks, fruit bins, netting and irrigation gear on the orchard and vineyard country running south toward the granite, and trade and building storage in town
access:
The approach matters here more than in most towns. Cunninghams Gap is a steep, tight climb through the Main Range with limited overtaking and a history of closures after landslips and heavy rain, and when it shuts the detour is a long way around. We watch it. If it is closed, or the weather looks like closing it, the load goes up the Toowoomba range and comes down the New England instead, which adds time but not drama. Either way it is half a day of driving before anything gets unloaded, so a firm delivery window matters more here than it does closer to home.

Once the truck is in the district, Warwick is one of the more cooperative towns to deliver into. The street grid is wide, properly wide, laid out with a bullock team in mind, and there is room to work in front of most town blocks without shutting anything down. Rural entries on the Downs country are long, straight and built for headers, and a side loader with a 40ft on it fits into that world comfortably.

The ground splits in two. North and west of town the Condamine flats are black cracking clay, the same reactive soil as the rest of the Downs: greasy in the wet, split open in the dry, and unforgiving to a loaded truck after rain. South and east, running toward the granite belt, the country turns to decomposed granite and sandy loam that drains fast and carries weight far better, but it has its own trick, because loose granitic gravel on a slope offers almost no grip at all.

Winter is the season to use. Warwick gets hard frosts and the ground goes bone-firm overnight, so a paddock that would bog a truck in February will carry it easily on a July morning. Summer storms are the opposite, and they can be very local, which means what happened on your place matters far more than the forecast for the town.

sections.h: Gear that lives on a truck half the year
p: The Southern Downs runs on a calendar. Campdrafts, rodeos, shows, sales and sale-day preparation fill a good part of the year, and the people who follow that circuit accumulate a specific kind of gear: saddlery, rugs, panels, ropes, feed, water gear, spare tyres, a generator. It is either on a truck or it is in the way. A container gives that a home it can be loaded out of and locked, which beats a tarp in the corner of a shed and beats storing it across three different places. The practical trick is where it sits: close enough to load from a float without carrying everything fifty metres, on ground firm enough to back up to in the wet, and with the doors facing the direction you will reverse in from rather than the direction that suited the delivery truck.

The same logic applies to contract work, which is the other half of how this district earns. Fencing contractors, shearing and crutching crews, spray operators, harvest contractors and builders all carry a plant list that has to be secure between jobs and does not fit in a ute. A 20ft on the home block, or a 10ft where the yard is tight, takes all of it off the ground and out of the weather. If the work moves, the container can move too. Units get relocated far more often than people expect when they buy their first one, which is worth thinking about at purchase, because a unit with a sound frame and undamaged corner castings picks up cleanly for the next twenty years and a tired one gets progressively more awkward to lift.

sections.h: Why a Warwick delivery gets locked in earlier
p: Warwick is far enough out that a delivery here is a planned day rather than an errand. The truck is committed once it leaves, and if something at the other end is wrong, a gate two hundred millimetres too narrow, a grid nobody trusts, a paddock that had forty millimetres on it overnight, the cost of that is a wasted day rather than a wasted hour. So we ask more questions before a Southern Downs run than we do before a local one, and we ask them earlier. Gate width, the surface from the gate to the spot, what is overhead, whether there is anywhere to turn a rigid or a semi, and what the weather has actually done on your place rather than in town.

The route gets decided the same morning if the Main Range is doubtful. Cunninghams Gap closes from time to time and it does not close by appointment. When it is out, the load goes the long way and the day gets longer. We would rather tell you that on the phone the day before than have a truck sitting at a road closure with your container on it. None of this means a Warwick delivery should be expected to be difficult, because most of them are not, but it is the reason we prefer a date with a bit of room in it to a promise of an hour.

sections.h: Grain, seed and fodder in a steel box
p: A container is very good at most agricultural storage and poor at one particular job, and it is worth being clear about which is which. Bagged seed, chemical, drums, fencing, water fittings, spare parts, vet supplies and baled hay all sit happily in a 20ft and stay dry, clean and locked. Loose bulk grain does not. The side walls of a shipping container are corrugated sheet designed to carry racking and torsion loads, not the outward pressure of several tonnes of wheat leaning against them, and grain brings its own moisture and sweats against cold steel on a Southern Downs night. If bulk grain is the problem, a silo is the answer. If the problem is everything else on the place currently living under a tarp or in the header shed, a container solves it for a good deal less than a new building, and it can be moved or sold on when the operation changes.

faqs.q: What happens if Cunninghams Gap is closed on my delivery day?
faqs.a: The load goes the other way, up the Toowoomba range and down the New England, and the day gets longer rather than cancelled. The Gap closes from time to time after heavy rain and landslips and it does not close by arrangement, so we check it before a Southern Downs run and ring you the day before if the timing is going to shift. It is the main reason we prefer to give a Warwick delivery a date with a bit of room in it rather than a promised hour on a promised morning.

faqs.q: Can you deliver onto black soil country around Warwick in the wet?
faqs.a: Not sensibly. The Condamine flats north and west of town are the same cracking clay as the rest of the Downs and they do not drain, so after decent rain the surface turns greasy and the material under it turns to putty. A loaded truck will bog and will cut ruts that last a season. We will move the date instead, which nobody out here finds surprising. If it is urgent, the alternative is to place the unit on the nearest hardstand or gravel and shift it across once the paddock has dried out.

faqs.q: Is the granite country south of Warwick easier to deliver onto?
faqs.a: In the wet, considerably. Decomposed granite and sandy loam drain fast and will carry a truck again within a day of rain that would shut black soil country down for most of a week. The trade-off is grip, because loose granitic gravel on a slope offers very little, and driveways through that country tend to be steeper and windier the closer you get to the ranges. The question changes from whether the ground will hold the truck to whether the truck can get up it and turn around once it is there.

faqs.q: Does a Warwick winter cause problems inside a container?
faqs.a: Cold on its own does not, but the swing does. Warwick gets hard frosts and clear days, so the steel drops well below the overnight air temperature and then climbs quickly, and moisture in the air inside condenses onto the roof and walls. Anything with batteries, electronics, paper or leather in it will notice over a season. Extra vents help, keeping the unit up off the ground helps, and loading things dry helps most of all. Do not store damp hay, green timber or wet canvas in a closed box and expect it to stay that way.

locations.name: Dalby
locations.depot: Loaded in the Lockyer Valley and run west on the Warrego
locations.leadTime: Usually three to five business days, and wet weather on unsealed roads moves it
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; 40ft on a side loader, and farm entries out here are generally built wide enough for it
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Dalby. Straight talk on black soil roads, harvest traffic, feedlots and laydown yards across the Western Downs.
locations.line: Everything about a delivery out here is decided by two things: the length of the run west, and whether it has rained. The road out is easy, sealed, straight, fast and busy with headers and road trains through harvest. The last few kilometres on black soil are the ones that matter, and they are the ones we ask about first.
locations.uses: grain, seed, chemical and fertiliser storage on cropping country, workshop and spare parts on feedlots and piggeries, laydown and tool storage for the gas field work north and west of town, cotton gear through the irrigation country toward Cecil Plains, fencing and water gear on grazing blocks, and site storage for the contractors who follow the harvest and the construction work through the district
access:
Black soil runs this district and it runs our delivery schedule with it. A Downs vertosol is a cracking clay that behaves like two entirely different materials depending on how much water is in it. Dry, it is close to concrete and you can drive anything on it. Wet, it does not drain. The surface turns to a grease that will not let a tyre grip and the material underneath turns to a putty a loaded rig will sink into and stay in. Councils close unsealed black soil roads outright after rain for exactly this reason and they are right to. A container delivery is not worth cutting up a road or a paddock for.

So the honest position is that we will give you a date and hold to it unless the weather says otherwise, and if it rains we move it rather than risk it. Everybody out here already works this way. Nobody is surprised.

When it is dry the deliveries are straightforward and often the easiest we do anywhere. Farm entries on the Downs are built for headers, chaser bins and B-doubles, so the gates are wide, the approaches are straight and there is usually somewhere sensible to turn around. The things to check are the ones invisible from the road: entry culverts and grids built a long time ago and never rated, powerlines crossing a paddock entrance at a height that suits a tractor but not a raised tilt tray, and the depth of the table drain either side of the gate.

Harvest is the other timing consideration. From about October the highway and the district roads fill with headers, chaser bins and grain trucks, and everyone on the place is flat out from before daylight. If a container is wanted in the middle of that, it is much better ordered before it starts.

sections.h: Steel on the gas fields
p: The Surat Basin work has put a particular kind of demand on containers across this district. Laydown yards need lockable storage that can be dropped where the work is and picked up again when it moves. Crews need a tool store that does not depend on there being a building. Site offices, first aid points, spares and consumables all end up in steel, because steel is the only thing that can be delivered complete, locked the same afternoon and relocated in a year without demolition. A container is a shipping unit before it is anything else, so it is built to be lifted, stacked, dragged onto a tray and set down on uneven ground repeatedly, which is exactly what site work asks of it.

What that use does demand is honesty about condition. A unit that will be lifted, moved and stacked needs a sound frame, corner castings that are not deformed, and a floor that has not been chewed out by forklift tynes. If a container is going to sit on a site for years and then move to the next one, it is worth spending up at the start. Where site rules apply, they generally decide the details: access times, inductions, whether a crane or telehandler is already on site, whether the unit has to sit on bearers. Put us in touch with whoever runs the gate and we will work to their requirements rather than turning up and finding out.

sections.h: Feedlots, piggeries and the parts problem
p: Intensive livestock changes the storage question. A feedlot or a piggery runs machinery that cannot be down for a week waiting on a part, so the operation carries spares, including belts, bearings, augers, hoses, pump ends and electrical gear, and those spares have to be somewhere dry, somewhere organised and somewhere that is not the middle of a workshop floor. A 20ft fitted out with shelving becomes the parts store, and because it is sealed and it locks, it keeps dust, rodents and casual borrowing out of the expensive end of the inventory.

Dust is the underrated one. Anywhere with stock, feed and traffic runs a permanent haze of fine dust that finds its way into everything, and it is much harder on bearings and electrical components than moisture is. A container with intact door seals sitting level is a genuinely tight box compared with an open-sided shed, and the difference shows up on the shelf after twelve months. Face the doors away from the prevailing westerly if the layout allows it, keep the unit off the ground so air moves underneath, and open it deliberately rather than leaving it swinging on a windy afternoon.

sections.h: Buying a container that will get moved again
p: Out here containers get relocated far more than most people expect. A unit bought for a block ends up at a shed, then at a work site, then back again, and every one of those moves puts the whole load through four corner castings. That is what they are for, but it makes condition matter in a specific way. Look at the frame and the castings before you look at the paint. A straight unit with sound castings and a solid floor lifts cleanly every time. As-is units are the cheaper end of the market and they are sold exactly as they stand. They are not sold as watertight, and some of them have been worked hard, which is fine for a fence-line lock-up that will never move again and a poor choice for something that has to be picked up twice a year. Every cargo-worthy unit we send out is checked wind and watertight before it leaves the yard, and if you want to see the actual unit first, photos are available on request and before delivery.

faqs.q: What happens if it rains before my delivery date?
faqs.a: It moves. Black soil roads and paddocks out here go from trafficable to impassable with one decent fall, and councils close unsealed black soil roads after rain for exactly that reason. We will not run a loaded truck onto country that is going to bog it and tear up your access, so we ring, we agree a new day, and we come when it has dried out. Everyone in this district already plans around that. If the timing is critical, order well ahead of when you need it rather than into a tight window.

faqs.q: Can you deliver during harvest?
faqs.a: Yes, but order earlier than you otherwise would. From about October the highway and the district roads fill with headers, chaser bins and grain trucks, everybody on the place is working long days, and finding a window where somebody can meet a truck at the gate gets harder than finding the truck. Deliveries still happen right through it. The failure mode is ringing on the Monday of a busy week and expecting Tuesday. Give it a bit of notice and harvest is not an obstacle at all.

faqs.q: Can you supply containers to gas field laydown yards and camps?
faqs.a: Yes. Site storage is a large part of what containers get used for across the Western Downs. Where a site has its own rules, those rules generally decide the details: access times, inductions, whether there is already a crane or a telehandler on site, and whether the unit has to sit on bearers. Put us in touch with whoever runs the gate and we will work to their requirements rather than turning up and finding out. Units that will be relocated repeatedly are worth buying in better condition than units that will never move.

faqs.q: How do we keep dust out of a container out here?
faqs.a: Most of the work is done by the unit itself, provided it is level and the door seals are intact, because a sound container is a far tighter box than an open-sided shed. Beyond that, face the doors away from the prevailing westerly if the layout allows it, sit it on sleepers or pads so it is off the ground and square, and open it deliberately rather than leaving it standing open on a windy afternoon. If it is holding electrical spares or bearings, a couple of sealed tubs inside finish the job.

locations.name: Chinchilla
locations.depot: Loaded at the Lockyer yard for the long run west on the Warrego
locations.leadTime: Usually four to seven business days, and we group loads heading that way
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; 40ft on a side loader, and on a long western run it often makes sense to send two units on the one trip
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Chinchilla. A planned run west on the Warrego, with real advice on black soil, sandy melon country and work sites.
locations.line: Chinchilla is a long day from the yard. Up over the range or around on the bypass, then west through the grain country with the highway running dead straight in front of you. That distance is the honest constraint here. It is also the reason we plan these deliveries properly rather than treating them as a run to the next town over.
locations.uses: melon and horticulture storage through the season, covering bins, picking gear, irrigation fittings and shade cloth, grain and chemical on the cropping blocks, laydown, tool and site storage for the gas industry work around the district, feedlot and cattle gear, workshop space on rural blocks a long way from the nearest hardware store, and secure storage for contractors working out of town for months at a stretch
access:
Two soils meet around Chinchilla and they behave nothing alike. The black cracking clay of the Western Downs runs through most of the cropping country and does what it does everywhere out here: carries anything when dry, turns to grease and putty when wet, and shuts access down for days rather than hours after a decent fall. Closer to the Condamine and through the melon country there is lighter sandy and red loam soil, which is the reason melons grow there in the first place. Sand drains fast and comes good quickly, but it is soft, and a loaded truck on dry deep sand can dig itself in just as effectively as one on wet clay. Two very different problems, and the answer to both is knowing which one you have before the truck leaves.

Distance shapes everything else. This is not a run where a truck can come back tomorrow if something is wrong, so we do the checking up front. Gate width, the surface from the gate to the spot, overhead lines, tree limbs, whether there is anywhere to turn around, and whether the ground has had rain on it in the last week. Photos of the approach sent through beforehand save more grief on a Chinchilla delivery than on any other page of this site.

Harvest and the industrial work in the district both put pressure on the roads at particular times of year, and the highway west of Dalby carries a lot of heavy vehicles that are not out there for the scenery. None of that stops a delivery. It just means an early start and a realistic window rather than a promise of an exact time.

Where a job is going onto a work site rather than a farm, the site rules generally decide the answer, and it is worth putting us in touch with whoever runs the gate before the day.

sections.h: Why we group loads heading west
p: Chinchilla is far enough from the yard that a single container on a truck is an inefficient way to move it, and the efficiency or otherwise of that trip ends up in your quote. So we plan western runs rather than improvising them. If there is another job going out the same week, your unit rides with it. If you want two units, they usually go together, and that is a better outcome than two separate trips a fortnight apart. Ordering with a week or so of notice, rather than needing it on Thursday, is the single thing that makes the most difference to what a Chinchilla delivery costs and how quickly it happens.

Freight to the Western Downs is quoted with the container rather than published, because it genuinely depends: how far past town you are, whether the last stretch is sealed, what has to be sent to do the job, and whether we can pair the trip with something else going the same way. One phone call gets you an exact number for your address rather than a range that turns into a different number later. Container prices we are happy to talk about openly. The truck is the part that changes with every single job, and pretending otherwise would only mean quoting you twice.

sections.h: Melon country, and the storage the season needs
p: Melons made this town's name and the season they run on is short and intense. When picking is on, everything is needed at once and there is nowhere to put anything. When it is over, there is a paddock full of bins, shade cloth, poly, fittings, sprayers and picking gear that has to survive until next year. Sunlight is the enemy in that gap. Poly pipe, drip tape, tarps and shade cloth degrade far faster sitting in the open through a Western Downs summer than they do in use, and replacing them is a real cost against a crop that has already been paid for once.

A container parked at the end of the packing area fixes that and does two other things as well. It gives you somewhere lockable for the gear that tends to walk, and it gives you a dry, vermin-resistant space without adding another permanent building to the yard. If it is going to hold anything that gasses off, or anything that has been put away with moisture still in it, get extra vents fitted at the yard before it goes out. Vents high in the side walls cost very little while the unit is in front of us and are an awkward job once it is sitting on your block, three hundred kilometres away.

sections.h: What to buy when the nearest replacement is a long way off
p: Distance should change what you buy. Close to a yard, a marginal container is a recoverable mistake, because we come back and swap it. Three hundred kilometres out, the same mistake costs a day of everybody's time, so the sensible play at this distance is to buy a grade above what you think you need. Cargo-worthy is the working standard: units assessed as fit to carry freight at sea, and every cargo-worthy container we send out is checked wind and watertight before it leaves the yard. One-trip units are close enough to new and are what people choose when the container is going somewhere it will be looked at, or is going to be cut into later. As-is units are cheaper for a reason, because they are sold in the condition they stand in and they are not sold as watertight, and while they suit plenty of jobs, sending one on a long haul to store something that matters is a false economy.

faqs.q: How far ahead should we order a container for Chinchilla?
faqs.a: A week or so of notice makes a real difference. This is a long run west and we plan those trips rather than improvising them, so notice lets your unit ride with another job going the same way, which is quicker for you and cheaper. Urgent is still possible. It just means a truck making the trip for one container. If you know a container is coming in the next month, ring now and take a date. Order it on the Wednesday you need it and you are effectively paying for the whole truck.

faqs.q: Can we get two containers delivered on one trip?
faqs.a: Usually, and out here it is well worth doing. Sending two units on a single western run is a far better outcome than two separate trips, and if a neighbour or somebody else in the district is buying at the same time it is worth mentioning, because pairing loads is straightforward when we know about it in advance and impossible once a truck has already gone. Tell us at the quote stage rather than after the first one is on the ground and we will build the run around it.

faqs.q: Will a container sit properly on sandy melon country?
faqs.a: It will, but sand behaves differently to clay and it needs a slightly different answer. Sand drains beautifully and comes good within a day of rain, which is a real advantage out here. What it does not do is spread a point load, so a corner casting sitting straight on dry deep sand will keep working its way in. Use wide bearing under the corners rather than small pads: full-length hardwood sleepers, or a decent concrete pad at each corner. Scrape back to firmer material first if there is any, and check it again after the first wet.

faqs.q: Can you deliver to a work camp or laydown yard around Chinchilla?
faqs.a: Yes. Site deliveries out here are routine and the site itself normally sets the terms: induction requirements, delivery windows, whether a crane or telehandler is available on site, and where the unit is allowed to sit. Give us a contact for whoever controls the gate and we will arrange it with them directly. If the unit is going to be moved around the site, or on to the next job afterwards, say so when you order, because the condition of the frame and corner castings matters much more for a container that gets lifted often.
